clue.text: Paper cash exchanged for pile of junk

indicators.note: things exchanged are swapped around, so these letters trade places into a new order

blocks.note: both words taken as written, nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone trades in banknotes and gets a heap of rubbish for their money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper cash exchanged' reads like a currency swap; it is the letters of those two words that get exchanged, making SCRAP HEAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap heap is literally a mound of discarded waste material, rubbish thrown together in one place.

clue.text: Quiet individual excelled

blocks.note: sh is the sound made to ask for quiet
a single individual is one

explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like a description of a modest high achiever; SH plus ONE gives SHONE.
explanation.definitionFit: To shine at something is an idiom for performing brilliantly, standing out from others by skill.

clue.text: Something that defends bit of Suffolk, Lincoln or Herdwick?

blocks.note: Suffolk, Lincoln and Herdwick are all British breeds of sheep, so a male of any of them is a ram
a bit of something is a part

explanation.surface: It sounds like a question about which English county or town has a defensive wall.
explanation.walkthrough: Suffolk and Lincoln look like places, but here they are sheep breeds alongside the Lake District's Herdwick; the question mark flags the definition by example. A bit of a sheep is a RAM PART.
explanation.definitionFit: A rampart is a broad defensive earth wall or bank around a fort, protecting those inside from attack.

clue.text: Rubbish underwear

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for something worthless or poor
second meaning: British word for underpants or knickers

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it is an insult about clothing. In British slang 'pants' means rubbish, and in Britain pants are underwear, not trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal usage calls bad things pants, and British English uses the same word for underpants worn beneath clothes.

clue.text: English proceed initially to Split for self-inflating experience

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
to proceed is to go
the first letter of this small word
to split or tear is to rip

explanation.surface: An English tourist heads off to Split in Croatia for a holiday that boosts the ego.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S dresses 'Split' as the Croatian port; it is the verb meaning tear.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego trip is an activity pursued mainly to boost one's own self-importance, puffing up vanity and pride.

clue.text: Fitting part of expert in entertainment

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is wanted, a run of consecutive letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, starting inside the first

explanation.surface: An expert fitter does a turn in a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside exPERT IN ENTertainment.
explanation.definitionFit: Pertinent means relevant or appropriate to the matter in hand, which is one sense of suitable or apt.

clue.text: Love lost in damp fog

indicators.note: something lost goes missing, so a letter disappears from inside the word that follows

blocks.note: damp means slightly wet, moist
love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A romance fades away in murky weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Take O out of MOIST to leave MIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Mist is a thin haze of tiny water droplets in the air, a light kind of fog.

clue.text: First of Man United passes over player's head creates handfuls of dirt

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter only
a head sits at the top, so the leading letter of the word is taken
to pass over something is to cover it, so one piece goes on either side of another

blocks.note: opening letter of the word
U is the usual abbreviation for United in team names
to pass away is to die
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A Manchester United move: the ball is passed over a player's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passes' looks like football but means dies, as in passes away; DIES wraps P after M and U.
explanation.definitionFit: Children make mud pies by pressing wet earth into lumps, so each is a handful of soil shaped by hand.

clue.text: Loot German journalist showed off

blocks.note: swag is a burglar's stolen goods
GER is an abbreviation for German
an editor, ED, is the crossword's usual journalist

explanation.surface: A German reporter flaunted the spoils.
explanation.walkthrough: Swag is old thieves' slang for stolen goods, and an editor is the crossword's stock journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: To swagger is to walk or behave arrogantly to impress others, a conspicuous kind of boasting display.

clue.text: Punctuation mark at end of invitation to party for soldier

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: a comma is a punctuation mark
last letter of the word
a do is an informal party

explanation.surface: Someone puts a full stop or exclamation at the bottom of a party invitation sent to a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' and 'to' just string the pieces together: COMMA, then N, then DO.
explanation.definitionFit: A commando is a member of an elite military unit trained for raids, so a kind of soldier.

clue.text: Change sketch of jailer after reflection

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front, so the letters are read the other way

blocks.note: a warder is a prison guard

explanation.surface: A prison guard thinks it over and alters a drawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After reflection' sounds like thinking it over; it means mirror-reversed, turning WARDER into REDRAW.
explanation.definitionFit: To redraw a picture is to make the drawing again differently, altering the earlier version.

clue.text: Goes off Mon-Fri around city area

indicators.note: to go around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: Monday to Friday are the working days
EC, East Central, is the postcode district covering the City of London

explanation.surface: A commuter leaves for work each weekday and travels round the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes off' looks like departing but means rots; EC is the London postcode for the City, its financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that goes off spoils and rots, which is to decay through natural decomposition.

clue.text: Calls about trouble in barrier

definitions.note: singular definition for a plural-looking answer; railings form one barrier

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: to ring someone is to call them on the phone
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Someone phones about a problem with a fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calls' looks like the main verb, but it is the outer piece, wrapped round the trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Railings are a fence of upright bars that blocks passage, so together they form a barrier.

clue.text: Hurry from hotel in guise of X

blocks.note: H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
dressed up as someone is in their guise
X is ten in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone flees a hotel disguised as a mysterious Mr X.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like a secret identity but is the Roman numeral for ten.
explanation.definitionFit: To hasten is to move or act quickly, a slightly formal synonym for rushing along.

clue.text: Praise song and dance on allotment

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits directly above it

blocks.note: making a song and dance is making a fuss, an ado
a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: Gardeners sing and dance in celebration on their vegetable plot.
explanation.walkthrough: An allotment in Britain is a rented garden plot, but here it means a share; 'song and dance' is the idiom for a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoration is worship or deep reverent esteem, the fullest form of glorifying someone.

clue.text: Lost again, wandering in state of wistfulness

indicators.note: something wandering strays from its path, so these letters drift into a new order

blocks.note: both words taken as written, nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone lost once more drifts about, feeling wistful.
explanation.walkthrough: LOST AGAIN rearranges to NOSTALGIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Nostalgia is a sentimental longing for the past, a bittersweet yearning for earlier times.

clue.text: President with certain force

blocks.note: PRES is a short form of president
certain means sure

explanation.surface: A head of state wields some kind of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certain force' reads as an adjective and noun; certain is SURE, joined to PRES.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressure is physical push exerted on something, or coercion applied to a person, both kinds of compulsion.

clue.text: See storm brewing somewhere in the south-west

indicators.note: brewing means mixing and fermenting, so these letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: both words taken as written, eight letters

explanation.surface: A weather forecaster watches a storm building over the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset is a county in south-west England; 'brewing' suits both a storm and the region's cider.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is an English county in the West Country, so it is one place in that south-western region.

clue.text: Controversial and revolutionary book I have

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the word is turned back to front

blocks.note: a tome is a large book
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: An author owns a radical, contentious book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary book' looks like a political text; 'revolutionary' only tells you to turn the book round.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotive issue arouses strong feeling, and such subjects tend to be hotly disputed.

clue.text: Trade vehicles

blocks.note: first meaning: dealing or commerce, often illicit
second meaning: the cars and lorries moving on roads

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a phrase for commercial vans; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic means buying and selling, as in drug traffic, and also the stream of cars and lorries using a road.

clue.text: Harangue one entering business

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: trade is business or commerce
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A boss lectures a newcomer joining the firm.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside TRADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech of criticism, essentially the same as a ranting lecture.

clue.text: Artist to draw relentlessly competitive way of life

blocks.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword's usual artist
to trace is to draw by copying lines

explanation.surface: A painter is driven to depict cutthroat modern living.
explanation.walkthrough: RA + TRACE regroups as RAT RACE.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is an idiom for the exhausting struggle for success in modern working life.

clue.text: Picture of old king wearing hat

indicators.note: something worn goes on the outside, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: a Panama is a light straw hat
O is a standard abbreviation for old
R is rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A portrait of a former monarch in a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: O + R sit inside PANAMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A panorama is a wide view of a scene, or a picture showing a broad sweeping vista.

clue.text: Humorous writing about following it and it returning

indicators.note: one thing following others comes after them, so it is placed last
returning means coming back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: it is slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
the word taken as written, then turned round
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A comic essay that keeps circling back on its own subject.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'it's do different jobs: the first is the crossword's sex appeal, the second is the word itself turned round; 'about' comes after both.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire is a form of comic writing that mocks folly or vice through irony and ridicule.

clue.text: Reason partners enter cathedral area

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a see is a bishop's diocese, centred on a cathedral
North and South are partners in bridge

explanation.surface: A couple go into a cathedral close for a reason.
explanation.walkthrough: North and South form a partnership at the bridge table, which is why 'partners' gives two compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: Sense means sound judgement or reasonableness, as in talking sense, close to logic and rationality.

clue.text: Stylish rector with appeal to unknowns

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for rector
it is slang for sex appeal
algebra uses x, y and z for unknown quantities

explanation.surface: A fashionable vicar appeals to strangers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' and 'to' just join R, IT and ZY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritzy, from the Ritz hotel, is informal for luxurious and glamorous, smartly fashionable.

clue.text: Broadcasting first-class band

blocks.note: A1 means first-class, with the 1 read as I
a ring is a band, for instance on a finger

explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks musical alongside broadcasting but is a ring; A1 becomes AI.
explanation.definitionFit: Airing a programme means transmitting it on radio or television, so the noun matches the gerund.

clue.text: Warm worker's sweets

blocks.note: warm feelings are fond ones
a worker ant, so worker's is ANT'S

explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' in crosswords is often an ant, a worker ant; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Fondants are soft creamy confections made from sugar paste, a type of candy.

clue.text: Stake and nails trainee employs initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives only its opening letter

blocks.note: opening letters of four words in turn

explanation.surface: A betting stake, and an apprentice uses nails at the start of a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stake' suggests a post being nailed; it is a gambler's stake.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker an ante is the bet each player puts into the pot before the deal.

clue.text: Nemesis of strangely cheery man

indicators.note: something done strangely is done oddly, so these letters come out in an unusual order

blocks.note: both words taken as written, nine letters

explanation.surface: An oddly cheerful man has a sworn foe.
explanation.walkthrough: CHEERY MAN rearranges to ARCH-ENEMY; a cheery man is an odd nemesis.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is a person's principal opponent or bitter rival, the foe who keeps returning.
